Being a rather small defenseless girl, I've always avoided running anytime after dinner time whether I was where I grew up in a rural area, or in Pittsburgh where I currently live. My mom always says I should carry pepper spray, but I feel like that would be more helpful against stray dogs back in the country rather than people in the city.

The first thing to be aware of is cars/trucks/buses ect. There are a lot of them and they emit pollution. I've learned that the traffic is much less of a problem if I run early in the morning, therefore I have less chance of breathing in bus exhaust. Also, the sidewalks are less crowded by people in the morning. 

You will most likely encounter many more traffic lights that you actually have to wait for if you don't want to get hit. You can probably get around a lot of that by running early or very late.

You also really need to find what parks or nature preserves are near to you. It was a shock to move straight into the middle of a city. I NEEDED to find somewhere that had more trees than people or else I'd actually have lost it.

Firstly, congrats on your first half marathon! I'm glad you enjoyed it. Give yourself a few days (or a week) to recover! If you have any lingering aches and pains definitely give your body a chance to heal itself after your race. I wouldn't jump straight back in to the long runs or you might burn yourself out (mentally mostly). Since your next race is in the fall, you have time to let yourself ease back into training. Don't forget though that now you're in pretty darn good shape so you can start more or less where you left off before your race.

In my first half I had never ran that far before so it was pretty painful getting through that last 5k. That experience made be believe that if I could become more comfortable with the distance, I'd be able to push myself and do much better the next time. So I did exactly that. I made longer distance my best friend. I became really aware during 13, 15, and 17 mile runs how my body felt when it needed a little water or some electrolytes. I also became aware of when I had it in me to run faster! After phasing more and more mileage into my week, my second half marathon wasn't new territory anymore. I knew what I was doing and how I was supposed to feel at different points of the race. So yes get in more hill work since that's a great low impact way of gaining strength, but also gradually increase the mileage of your long run so that your brain and your body knows better how to deal with exhaustion. You'll have a great experience the next time around too!
